usage: 전등 + 을 + 켜다; 켜다 is the on-verb for any light/device
전등 + 을 + 끄다; 끄다 is the matching off-verb
전등 + 을 + 갈다; 갈다 = swap an old one for new
examples: 방이 어두워요. 전등을 켜요.
The room is dark. I'll turn on the light.
Basic cause→action: 어둡다 (dark) leads to 켜다 (turn on).
나갈 때 전등 꺼 주세요.
Please turn off the light when you go out.
꺼 주세요 = polite request; in casual speech 불 꺼 is even more common.
거실 전등이 자꾸 깜빡거려서 새것으로 갈았어요.
The living-room light kept flickering, so I replaced it with a new one.
깜빡거리다 = flicker; real-life maintenance situation.
nuance: 전등 is Sino-Korean: 電 (electric) + 燈 (lamp), literally 'electric lamp' — the fixed electric light of a room, typically the ceiling light. The crucial register point: 전등 is the technical/written word, but in real conversation Koreans almost always just say 불 ('fire/light'), as in 불 켜 / 불 꺼. Saying 전등을 켜 주세요 is understood but sounds stiff; 불 좀 켜 줄래? is how people actually talk. Contrast with 조명, which means lighting as a concept or mood (무대 조명 'stage lighting', 조명이 예뻐요 'the lighting is pretty'), whereas 전등 is the physical fixture. The English pitfall is reaching for 열다/닫다 (open/close) because English says 'turn the light on'; lights take 켜다/끄다, never 열다. Also note 전등 is the whole light fixture, not the bulb (전구) that screws inside it.

Over-using 전등 in conversation sounds textbook-stiff. For everyday 'turn the light on/off', native speakers say 불 켜다 / 불 끄다.
Confusing 전등 (the fixture/lamp) with 전구 (the bulb inside it). You replace a burnt-out 전구, not the whole 전등, when only the bulb dies.

usage: 전구 + 를 + 갈다; the standard verb for swapping a bulb
to screw in / fit the bulb
전구 + 를 + 끼우다 = insert into the socket
전구 + 한 개; count bulbs with the general counter 개
examples: 전구가 나갔어요.
The light bulb burned out.
Simple state result: 나가다 here = stop working, not 'go outside'.
전구가 나가서 새것으로 갈았어요.
The bulb died, so I changed it for a new one.
나가서 (because it died) + 갈다 (replace) — the everyday repair phrasing.
이 스탠드는 전구를 돌려서 끼우면 돼요.
For this lamp, you just screw the bulb in by turning it.
돌려서 끼우다 = turn-and-fit; real instruction-giving register.
nuance: 전구 is Sino-Korean 電 (electric) + 球 (ball/globe), literally 'electric globe' — named for the round glass shape, and it means specifically the screw-in bulb, not the whole fixture (전등). The key idiom learners must memorize is 전구가 나갔어요 for 'the bulb burned out': 나가다 literally means 'go out', and Korean treats a dead bulb as the light having 'gone out', much like English 'the light went out'. To install a fresh one you 갈다 (replace) or 끼우다 (fit/insert). The English-speaker pitfall is saying 전구가 죽었어요 ('the bulb died') by direct-translating English slang — Koreans don't use 죽다 for bulbs; it sounds odd and even slightly comic. Also don't use 깨지다 (shatter) unless the glass actually broke; a simply non-working bulb 나갔어요 even though it looks intact.

usage: to turn on the desk lamp
스탠드 + 를 + 켜다; same on-verb as any light
to turn off the desk lamp
책상(desk) + 스탠드, a compound naming where it sits
스탠드 + 불빛; 불빛 = the light a lamp gives off
examples: 책 읽을 때 스탠드를 켜요.
I turn on the desk lamp when I read.
Basic habit; 읽을 때 = when (I) read.
눈 아프니까 천장등 끄고 스탠드만 켜자.
My eyes hurt, so let's turn off the ceiling light and use just the desk lamp.
Contrasts 천장등 (ceiling light) with 스탠드 (desk lamp); ~만 = only.
밤에는 은은한 스탠드 불빛이 좋아요.
At night I like the soft glow of a desk lamp.
은은하다 = soft/mellow (of light); a mood-describing real sentence.
nuance: 스탠드 is a 'Konglish' loanword from English 'stand', but its meaning has narrowed in Korean to one thing: a desk or table lamp for reading and studying. This is a false-friend trap — an English speaker hears 'stand' and pictures a rack, a stadium stand, or a place to stand, but in a Korean home 스탠드 means the small reading lamp. The fuller forms 전기스탠드 (electric stand) and 스탠드 조명 exist, yet plain 스탠드 is by far the most common. Contrast it with 전등, which is the fixed ceiling light of the whole room: you switch off the 전등 and leave just the 스탠드 on for cozy late-night light. It uses the universal light verbs 켜다/끄다, and its glow is described with 불빛 plus adjectives like 은은하다 (soft) or 따뜻하다 (warm). Don't try to say 'I stand' with this noun — that idea is the verb 서다.

usage: to look at / check the calendar
달력 + 을 + 보다, the default verb for consulting it
to mark it on the calendar
달력 + 에 + 표시하다; 에 = the location of the mark
to flip the calendar (to the next month)
달력 + 을 + 넘기다 = turn the page over
examples: 달력 좀 봐 줄래요?
Could you check the calendar for me?
Simple polite request; 좀 softens it.
약속 날짜를 달력에 표시해 뒀어요.
I marked the appointment date on the calendar.
표시해 두다 = mark and leave it (for later); ~에 marks where.
벌써 12월이라 새 달력으로 바꿔야 해요.
It's already December, so I have to switch to a new calendar.
Real year-end situation; 바꾸다 = swap out.
nuance: 달력 is a hybrid word — native 달 (month/moon) plus Sino-Korean 曆 (력, calendar/almanac) — and it means the physical printed calendar: the grid of dates you hang on the wall (벽걸이 달력) or stand on a desk (탁상 달력). The sharp distinction English speakers miss is calendar-the-object vs schedule-the-plan. 달력 is only the dated paper grid; your personal plans, appointments, and agenda live in your 일정 (schedule) or 다이어리/플래너 (planner), and on your phone in a 캘린더 app. So 'add it to my calendar' meaning your appointments is 일정에 추가하다, NOT 달력에 추가하다. You 보다 (look at) a 달력 to check a date, 표시하다 to mark a day, and 넘기다 to flip to the next month. Beware also of the bare syllable 달, which alone means 'the moon' or 'a month' — 달력 is the printed object, never the moon.

Saying 달력을 읽다 ('read the calendar'). You 보다 (look at) a calendar to check a date; 읽다 (read) suits text, not a date grid.

usage: 액자 + 를 + 걸다, for putting it on a wall
to put (a photo) into the frame
사진 + 을 + 액자 + 에 + 넣다; 에 = into where
사진(photo) + 액자, names what it holds
to slot/fit (a photo) into the frame
액자 + 에 + 끼우다 = fit snugly in
examples: 이 액자 정말 예쁘다.
This frame is really pretty.
Casual admiration; 예쁘다 describes the frame itself.
가족사진을 액자에 넣어서 책상에 놨어요.
I put the family photo in a frame and set it on the desk.
넣다(put in) + 놓다(set down) chained with ~어서.
결혼사진을 큰 액자에 넣어서 거실 벽에 걸었어요.
I framed our wedding photo and hung it on the living-room wall.
Real-life decorating; note 액자에 넣다 then 벽에 걸다.
nuance: 액자 is Sino-Korean 額 (frame/tablet) + 子 (a noun-forming suffix), and it means the frame that holds a photo or picture — the kind you stand on a shelf or hang on a wall. The essential separation for learners is container vs content: the 액자 is the empty frame, while the 사진 (photo) or 그림 (picture/painting) is what goes inside it. So you 넣다 (put) or 끼우다 (fit) a 사진 into an 액자, and you 걸다 (hang) the 액자 on the wall. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb for hanging: use 걸다, not 붙이다. 붙이다 means to stick/affix something flat and adhesive (a poster, a sticker, tape), whereas a framed picture hangs from a hook, which is 걸다 — and its resting state is 걸려 있다 ('is hanging'). Don't confuse 액자 with 틀, the generic word for a frame/mold/framework; 액자 is specifically the decorative picture frame.

Swapping 액자 (the frame) and 사진 (the photo inside). You put the 사진 into the 액자 — they are not the same word.
Saying 액자를 만들다 to mean 'take/frame a photo'. To frame a picture you 사진을 액자에 넣다; 만들다 would literally mean to build the frame from scratch.

usage: 화분 + 에 + 물 + 을 + 주다; literally 'give water to the pot'
화분 + 을 + 옮기다 = relocate it (e.g. for sunlight)
examples: 창가에 화분이 있어요.
There's a potted plant by the window.
Basic location; 창가 = the windowside.
화분에 물 주는 거 잊지 마세요.
Don't forget to water the plants.
Reminder register; 물 주다 = water, ~는 거 nominalizes the action.
집들이 선물로 작은 화분을 받았어요.
I got a small potted plant as a housewarming gift.
Real custom: 화분 is a classic 집들이(housewarming) gift.
nuance: 화분 is Sino-Korean 花 (flower) + 盆 (basin/pot), literally 'flower basin', and it refers to the planter together with whatever grows in it — both the pot and the potted plant as a set. Learners must keep three words apart: 꽃 is the flower (the bloom), 식물 is a plant in general, and 화분 is specifically the potted container-plant. The signature collocation is 화분에 물을 주다 — note Korean 'gives water TO the pot' (화분에... 주다), so the pot takes the particle 에 as the recipient/destination of the water. The English-speaker pitfall is the watering verb: never say 화분이 물을 마시다 ('the pot drinks water'). 마시다 (drink) is only for living beings consuming liquid by mouth; you 주다 (give) water to plants. Another natural verb is 키우다 (to raise/grow), the same verb used for pets and children, reflecting that you 'tend' a plant. To rearrange them you 옮기다 (move).

usage: 쿠션 + 을 + 안다; 안다 = hold in your arms
소파(sofa) + 쿠션, names where it lives
the cushion is soft and fluffy
쿠션 + 이/가 + 푹신하다, the signature texture word
쿠션 + 에 + 기대다; 에 marks what you lean on
examples: 소파에 쿠션이 많아요.
There are lots of cushions on the sofa.
Simple existence + quantity; 많다 = many.
쿠션 안고 텔레비전 봐요.
I watch TV hugging a cushion.
Common cozy habit; 안고 = while hugging (sequential ~고).
이 쿠션 진짜 푹신해서 베개 대신 써요.
This cushion is so fluffy I use it instead of a pillow.
푹신하다 (fluffy) + 대신 (instead of); hints at the 쿠션/베개 contrast.
nuance: 쿠션 is a loanword from English 'cushion' and means a soft throw cushion or decorative pillow you put on a sofa, bed, or chair to lean on, hug, or prop yourself up. The boundary learners must draw is against two near-neighbors. First, 베개 is specifically the pillow you sleep on with your head — a 쿠션 is for sitting and leaning, a 베개 is for sleeping, even though both are soft and stuffed. Second, 방석 is the flat floor cushion you sit ON (traditional in Korean homes for sitting on the heated floor), whereas a 쿠션 is something you hold or lean against. The defining adjective is 푹신하다 (soft-and-fluffy), the texture word that pairs with cushions and good mattresses; you 안다 (hug) a cushion or 기대다 (lean on) it. The pitfall is reaching for 베개 because English loosely calls both 'pillow' — keep 쿠션 (throw cushion) and 베개 (sleeping pillow) distinct.

Describing it as 부드럽다 only. 부드럽다 means smooth/soft to the touch (skin, fabric); the springy 'fluffy' feel of a cushion is 푹신하다.

usage: to cover oneself with a blanket
(몸에) 담요 + 를 + 덮다; drape it over you
담요 + 를 + 개다; 개다 = fold bedding/cloth neatly
무릎(knee/lap) + 담요, names where you use it
담요 + 를 + 덮어 + 주다 = cover someone as a kindness
examples: 추워서 담요를 덮었어요.
It was cold, so I covered up with a blanket.
Basic cause→action; 추워서 = because it's cold.
무릎에 담요 덮을래요?
Would you like a blanket over your knees?
Offering register; 무릎에 = onto the lap, ~ㄹ래요 = soft offer.
비행기에서 승무원이 담요를 가져다줬어요.
On the plane the flight attendant brought me a blanket.
Real situation; 가져다주다 = bring (and give) — 담요 is the airplane/throw blanket.
nuance: 담요 is a light blanket or throw — the thinner cover you drape over your lap, shoulders, or knees when you feel chilly (on a sofa, a plane, at a desk). The contrast every learner needs is 담요 vs 이불: 이불 is the thick quilt/duvet/comforter you sleep under in bed at night, while 담요 is the lighter, smaller throw for warmth while awake. So you 'snuggle under the 이불' to sleep but 'put a 담요 over your lap' while watching TV. Two verb pitfalls stand out. For putting it over yourself, use 덮다 (to cover over) — not 입다 (wear), since a blanket isn't clothing. For tidying it away, use 개다, the specific verb for folding bedding and laundry, NOT 접다. 접다 is for folding paper, a map, or an umbrella along creases; soft bedding is 개다. To cover someone else kindly, the giving form 담요를 덮어 주다 adds the nuance of doing it for them.

mistakes: Folding a blanket with 접다. 접다 is for paper/maps/umbrellas; soft bedding and laundry are folded with 개다 → 담요를 개다.
Confusing 담요 (light throw, used while awake) with 이불 (thick sleeping quilt/duvet). You sleep under an 이불; you drape a 담요 over your lap.
Saying 담요를 입다 ('wear the blanket'). A blanket isn't clothing; you 덮다 (cover) yourself with it → 담요를 덮어요.

usage: to throw it in the trash can
쓰레기 + 를 + 쓰레기통 + 에 + 버리다; 에 = into where
쓰레기통 + 을 + 비우다 = make it empty
쓰레기통 + 이/가 + 가득 차다 = filled to the brim
음식물(food matter) + 쓰레기통, a sorted-waste type
examples: 쓰레기통이 어디 있어요?
Where's the trash can?
Basic location question; very common phrase.
휴지는 쓰레기통에 버려 주세요.
Please throw the tissue in the trash can.
버리다 = throw away; ~에 marks the destination.
쓰레기통이 가득 차서 비웠어요.
The trash can was full, so I emptied it.
가득 차다 (be full) + 비우다 (empty) — the natural pair.
nuance: 쓰레기통 is a transparent compound: 쓰레기 (trash/garbage) + 통 (bin/barrel/container), so 'trash container' = wastebasket/trash can. The verb you must lock in is 버리다 (throw away/discard), and the trash can takes 에 as the destination: 쓰레기통에 버리다 ('throw into the trash can'). The big English-speaker pitfall is 던지다: English 'throw it in the trash' makes learners pick 던지다, but 던지다 means to hurl/toss something through the air (a ball, a stone). Discarding garbage is 버리다, an act of disposal, not a throwing motion. A culturally important note: Korea strictly sorts waste, so beyond the general 쓰레기통 you'll meet 음식물 쓰레기통 (food waste), 재활용(품) / 분리수거함 (recycling bins), and 일반 쓰레기 (general waste) — putting things in the right bin matters. Finally, 쓰레기통 is written as one word with no internal space, and you 비우다 (empty) it when it 가득 차다 (gets full).

usage: 빗자루 + 로 + 쓸다; 로 = with/using the tool
to sweep the floor with a broom
바닥(floor) + 을 + 쓸다, the typical target
빗자루 + 질(act of) + 하다 = the act of broom-using
빗자루 + 와 + 쓰레받기, the standard pairing
examples: 빗자루로 바닥을 쓸어요.
I sweep the floor with a broom.
Core sentence; note the 로(with) + 을(object) frame.
빗자루랑 쓰레받기 좀 갖다줄래요?
Could you bring me the broom and dustpan?
Real request; 빗자루 almost always teams with 쓰레받기.
마당에 낙엽이 많아서 빗자루로 싹 쓸었어요.
There were lots of leaves in the yard, so I swept them all up with a broom.
싹 = clean/completely (sweeping adverb); 마당 = yard.
nuance: 빗자루 is the broom you sweep floors and yards with, and its inseparable verb is 쓸다 (to sweep), with the tool marked by 로/으로: 빗자루로 쓸다 ('sweep with a broom'). It naturally travels with its partner 쓰레받기 (dustpan) — you sweep the dust into the dustpan. The central English-speaker pitfall is mixing up cleaning verbs: 쓸다 (sweep, with a broom) versus 닦다 (wipe, with a cloth) versus 쓸다's lookalike tasks. Sweeping loose dirt/dust off a floor is 쓸다; wiping a surface clean with a rag is 닦다 — don't say 빗자루로 닦다. A second trap is the near-homonym 빗 (a hair comb) and 빗다 (to comb one's hair): 빗자루 (broom) and 빗 (comb) share the 빗 syllable and even the brushing image, but they are different objects — you 빗으로 머리를 빗다 (comb hair with a comb) but 빗자루로 바닥을 쓸다 (sweep the floor with a broom). The act of sweeping can also be nominalized as 빗자루질 / 비질.

Marking the broom with 을/를 as if it's what you sweep. The broom is the instrument → 로/으로: 빗자루로 바닥을 쓸어요.

usage: 걸레 + 를 + 빨다; 빨다 = wash cloth/laundry
걸레 + 질(act of) + 하다 = do floor-wiping
걸레 + 를 + 짜다 = squeeze water out
examples: 걸레로 바닥을 닦아요.
I wipe the floor with a rag.
Core sentence; 로(with) + 을(object) again.
걸레가 더러워서 빨아서 짰어요.
The rag was dirty, so I washed and wrung it out.
빨다(wash) → 짜다(wring), the natural sequence with ~서.
물 쏟았으니까 걸레로 좀 닦아 줄래?
I spilled water, so could you wipe it up with a rag?
Casual request; 쏟다 = spill — a real trigger for grabbing a 걸레.
nuance: 걸레 is the cleaning rag or floor cloth used for the dirty work of wiping floors and surfaces, paired with the verb 닦다 (to wipe) and the tool particle 로: 걸레로 닦다. The act of mopping/wiping the floor with it is 걸레질. Two contrasts are essential. By cloth-type: a 걸레 is a grubby floor/cleaning rag (low-status, gets filthy), 행주 is a clean dishcloth for wiping the kitchen counter and dishes, and 수건 is a towel for drying your body — Koreans keep these strictly separate, and calling a kitchen cloth a 걸레 sounds unhygienic. (Note: 걸레 is also a strong insult when applied to a person, so use it only for the object.) The big verb pitfall is washing it: a dirty rag is cleaned with 빨다 (the verb for washing cloth and laundry), NOT 씻다. 씻다 is for washing your body or rinsing dishes/produce; fabric is 빨다. After washing you 짜다 (wring) it. Don't confuse the wiping verb either: 걸레로 닦다 (wipe), not 쓸다 (which needs a broom).

usage: 다리미 + 로 + 다리다; tool 로 + the verb 다리다
셔츠(shirt) + 를 + 다리다, a typical target
다리미 + 이/가 + 뜨겁다, the key safety adjective
다리미 + 를 + 켜다 = switch it on to heat
examples: 다리미로 셔츠를 다려요.
I iron the shirt with the iron.
Core sentence; note tool 다리미로 + verb 다리다.
다리미 뜨거우니까 조심해요.
The iron's hot, so be careful.
뜨겁다(hot) + 조심하다(be careful) — the standard warning.
면 셔츠는 주름이 잘 가서 매번 다리미로 다려야 해요.
Cotton shirts wrinkle easily, so I have to iron them every time.
주름이 가다 = get wrinkles; ~아야 하다 = have to.
nuance: 다리미 is the clothes iron — the appliance — and it derives from the verb 다리다 (to iron) plus the instrument-forming suffix -이, so it literally means 'the thing for ironing'. This built-in relationship is exactly the trap: the noun 다리미 (the iron) and the verb 다리다 (to iron) look and sound nearly identical, and learners constantly blur them. Lock the pattern as 다리미로 다리다 — 'iron WITH the iron', tool marked by 로, action by the verb 다리다. A second, classic homophone-style pitfall is 다리, which is a completely different word meaning 'leg' or 'bridge' (and the verb 달이다 'to brew/decoct medicine' sounds close too) — only 다리미/다리다 concern clothes. Note the irregular-looking conjugation of the verb: 다리다 → 다려요 (the 이+어 contracts to 여). The iron's defining adjective is 뜨겁다 (hot), and you 켜다 (turn on) the iron to heat it; the ironing board it sits on is a separate item, 다리미판.

Conjugating the verb as 다리어요. 다리다 contracts to 다려요 in the polite present (이 + 어 → 여).

usage: 벽시계 + 를 + 걸다, since it hangs on a wall
a wall clock is hanging on the wall
벽 + 에 + 걸려 있다 = is in a hung state
벽시계 + 이/가 + 멈추다, often when the battery dies
to change the wall clock's battery
examples: 거실에 벽시계가 있어요.
There's a wall clock in the living room.
Basic existence + location.
벽시계 보니까 벌써 세 시네요.
Looking at the wall clock, it's already three o'clock.
보니까 = upon looking; ~네요 = mild realization.
벽시계가 멈춰서 건전지를 갈았어요.
The wall clock stopped, so I changed the battery.
멈추다(stop) → 건전지 갈다(change battery): the typical fix.
nuance: 벽시계 is a transparent compound, 벽 (wall) + 시계 (clock/watch), so 'wall clock'. The base 시계 is itself Sino-Korean (時計, 'time-measure') and is the family root for a whole set of timepieces: 손목시계 (wrist + clock = wristwatch), 알람시계 / 자명종 (alarm clock), 탁상시계 (desk clock), 모래시계 (sand clock = hourglass), and 해시계 (sun clock = sundial). The English-speaker pitfall is that English splits 'clock' (on a wall/desk) from 'watch' (on the wrist), but Korean uses one word 시계 for both and just prefixes the location: a watch is literally a 'wrist-clock', 손목시계. As an object that hangs, a 벽시계 takes 걸다 (hang) and rests as 걸려 있다 ('is hanging'), exactly like a 액자 or 달력. When it 멈추다 (stops), the usual cause is a dead 건전지 (battery), which you 갈다 (replace). To 'check the time', you 시계를 보다 (look at the clock).

usage: to lay down / spread out a mat
매트 + 를 + 깔다; 깔다 = spread flat on a surface
매트 + 위에서 + 운동하다; 위에서 = on top of (action)
현관(entryway) + 매트, names where it lies
examples: 바닥에 매트를 깔았어요.
I laid a mat on the floor.
Core sentence; 깔다 is THE verb for spreading a flat thing down.
아기가 매트 위에서 기어 다녀요.
The baby crawls around on the mat.
위에서 = on top of (with motion); 기어 다니다 = crawl about.
운동할 거라서 요가 매트부터 깔았어요.
Since I'm going to work out, I laid out the yoga mat first.
Real prep sequence; ~부터 = (starting) with, ~ㄹ 거라서 = because I'm going to.
nuance: 매트 is a loanword from English 'mat' and covers the family of flat floor mats: 요가 매트 (yoga mat), 현관 매트 (doormat), a baby's play mat, a bath mat, a camping mat. Its signature verb is 깔다, the specific motion of spreading something flat across a surface — you 매트를 깔다 (lay/spread a mat), the same verb used for spreading out bedding (이불을 깔다) or a picnic blanket. The English-speaker pitfall here is verb choice: don't say 매트를 놓다. 놓다 means to set/place a discrete object down on a surface (a cup, a book), whereas a flat sheet that you spread out is 깔다. A second trap is the near-loanword 매트리스 (mattress): a thin floor mat is 매트, but the thick sprung bed you sleep on is 매트리스 — close in sound, different objects. When marking where action happens on the mat, use 위에서 (on top of, for an activity like exercising or playing); plain 위에 marks static location ('on the mat').
